## Simple explanation

A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a neural network that uses
convolution operations to detect local patterns in data such as images.
Early layers may detect simple patterns, while later layers combine them
into more complex features.

## Technical explanation

CNNs commonly combine convolutional layers, nonlinear activations, and
downsampling or pooling. A convolution applies a shared kernel across
positions, producing feature maps. Modern architectures may also include
normalization, residual connections, and attention.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

CNNs have been widely used for image classification, object detection,
medical imaging, and other spatial tasks. Their local connectivity and
weight sharing can make them effective for images, although architecture
choice depends on data, accuracy, latency, and deployment constraints.

## How it works

A filter slides over an input and computes a weighted combination of local
values. Multiple filters produce feature maps. Nonlinearities and
subsequent layers combine those features into representations used for
prediction.

## Practical example

A pretrained CNN can be fine-tuned to classify images as penguins or
ostriches. The [binary-classification notebook](../../notebooks/B/binary-classification.ipynb)
provides a code-free fast.ai scaffold for building that classifier.

## Common misconceptions

- A convolutional network does not automatically understand image meaning.
- CNNs are not restricted to images, although image processing is a common
  application.
- More layers do not guarantee better performance on a particular dataset.
